common_name: Snowcap Shasta Daisy (Compact Long-Blooming Dwarf Shasta Daisy)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall; Snowcap's compact, tidy habit makes it well suited to front-of-border placement and containers where taller Shasta cultivars would flop. Deadhead spent blooms regularly to prolong flowering from early to late summer.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Snowcap is a compact, heavy-blooming Shasta daisy bred by Alan Bloom at Bressingham, one of the shortest and most floriferous Shasta cultivars available, producing masses of classic single white daisy flowers with bright yellow centers on sturdy, non-flopping stems that rarely need staking. The dwarf, dense habit makes it far more useful than taller Shasta daisies for edging, mixed containers, and the front of a perennial border, while still delivering the abundant summer-long bloom the species is known for. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor and flower quality.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Leucanthemum Cultivars

common_name: Daisy May Shasta Daisy (Compact Early-Blooming Proven Winners Shasta Daisy)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or divisions in spring or fall. Daisy May blooms earlier than most Shasta daisy cultivars and continues over a long season if deadheaded; its compact, well-branched habit needs no staking.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; Daisy May is a compact, floriferous Shasta daisy selection introduced through the Proven Winners perennial line, valued for its early bloom start, tidy self-branching habit, and abundant classic white single flowers with golden centers held on strong stems that resist flopping in wind and rain. The extended bloom season and reliable performance across a range of climates have made it one of the most widely planted modern Shasta daisy cultivars. Divide clumps every two to three years in spring to keep plants vigorous and prevent the centers from thinning out.
sources: Proven Winners — Daisy May Shasta Daisy

common_name: Banana Cream Shasta Daisy (Pale Yellow Fading to Cream-White Shasta Daisy)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall. Flower color shifts from soft butter-yellow in bud and early bloom to pale cream and finally near-white as flowers age, so plants display several tones at once during peak bloom.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; Banana Cream, developed by Terra Nova Nurseries, is a Shasta daisy selection notable for flowers that open a soft pastel yellow and gradually fade through cream to white as they mature, giving the plant an unusual multi-tone effect rather than the pure white of most Shasta cultivars. The compact, well-branched habit and sturdy stems hold up well without staking, and the soft coloring blends easily with both pastel and white garden schemes. Deadhead regularly to prolong bloom and divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring.

common_name: Wirral Supreme Shasta Daisy (Classic Double-Flowered Heirloom Shasta Daisy)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall. Wirral Supreme is an older, well-tested cultivar that benefits from division every two to three years to maintain the quality and fullness of its double flowers.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Wirral Supreme is a long-established double-flowered Shasta daisy cultivar, first introduced in England in the 1920s and still widely grown for its full, shaggy, pure-white double blooms with a small cluster of yellow disc florets peeking from the center. The flowers are larger and fuller than single-form Shasta daisies, giving a more opulent, old-fashioned cottage-garden effect, and they hold up well as cut flowers. A reliable, garden-worthy heirloom that has earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit for its consistent performance and hardiness.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Leucanthemum x superbum 'Wirral Supreme' AGM

common_name: Cobham Gold Shasta Daisy (Creamy Yellow Semi-Double Shasta Daisy)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall. Flowers open pale creamy yellow and fade to near-white as they age, so newly opened and older blooms display together for a soft two-tone effect.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Cobham Gold is a semi-double Shasta daisy cultivar bearing ruffled, creamy pale-yellow flowers that gradually fade to white as they mature, a softer and more unusual coloring than the crisp pure white typical of the species. The sturdy, upright stems and long bloom season make it a reliable choice for the summer perennial border and cutting garden, and it has been recognized with the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. Divide clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor and flower size.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Leucanthemum x superbum 'Cobham Gold' AGM

common_name: Amethyst in Snow Mountain Cornflower (White Perennial Cornflower with Purple Center)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall. After the main late-spring flush, shear plants back to fresh foliage to encourage a possible second bloom in late summer and to keep the clump tidy.

directions: Plant in moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Amethyst in Snow is a striking bicolor selection of mountain cornflower bearing large, spidery white flowers with a contrasting deep reddish-purple center, a dramatic departure from the solid violet-blue of the species and one of the most distinctive perennial cornflower cultivars available. The soft gray-green, woolly foliage forms an attractive spreading mound beneath the flowers, which appear from late spring into early summer. Like the species, it spreads by rhizomes and can self-sow; deadhead before seed set if a more restrained clump is desired, and divide every two to three years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Gold Bullion Mountain Cornflower (Golden Foliage Perennial Cornflower)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall in a site with some afternoon shade in hot climates, since the golden foliage can scorch in intense full sun.

directions: Plant in moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade, with light afternoon shade recommended in hot-summer regions to prevent leaf scorch; Gold Bullion is a foliage-forward selection of mountain cornflower grown as much for its bright chartreuse-gold leaves as for its classic violet-blue, spidery cornflower blooms, which appear in late spring and provide vivid color contrast against the golden foliage backdrop. The compact mounding habit is lower and tidier than the species, making it useful as a bright accent along a border edge or in a foliage-color planting scheme. Shear back after the first flush of bloom to refresh foliage color and encourage a second flowering later in the season; divide every two to three years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Jubilee Gem Bachelor's Button (Dwarf Double AAS-Winning Cornflower)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, or sow in fall in mild-winter regions for earlier, bigger spring bloom. The compact, well-branched habit needs no staking, unlike taller cornflower types.

directions: Direct sow seed a half-inch deep in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Jubilee Gem is a historic dwarf cornflower cultivar, winner of the All-America Selections award in 1937, prized for its compact, sturdy, well-branched habit and fully double, deep cornflower-blue blooms produced in great abundance over a long season. Its short stature sets it apart from most cornflower varieties, which tend to grow tall and lanky and often require staking; Jubilee Gem stays neat and self-supporting, making it well suited to containers, edging, and the front of a cutting garden bed. Deadhead regularly to extend bloom, and expect the plants to decline once summer heat sets in, as cornflowers are a true cool-season annual.

common_name: Blue Diadem Cornflower (Extra-Large Deep Blue Heirloom Bachelor's Button)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter or early spring, or sow in fall in mild-winter regions for an earlier, larger spring display. The tall stems benefit from twiggy brush support or planting among neighboring perennials in windy sites.

directions: Direct sow seed a half-inch deep in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Blue Diadem is a classic English heirloom cornflower cultivar noted for producing the largest flowers of any blue-flowered cornflower variety, with fully double, densely packed blooms in a rich, saturated cornflower-blue held on tall, upright stems well above the narrow gray-green foliage. The exceptional flower size and deep color have made it a long-standing favorite for cutting gardens and cottage-style borders. Deadhead regularly to prolong bloom through late spring and early summer, and expect plants to decline with the arrival of hot weather, as cornflowers are a true cool-season annual.

common_name: Snowman Cornflower (Tall Heirloom White Bachelor's Button)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter or early spring, or sow in fall in mild-winter regions for a bigger, earlier spring bloom. Tall stems benefit from twiggy brush support or close neighboring plants in exposed sites.

directions: Direct sow seed a half-inch deep in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Snowman is a classic English heirloom cornflower selected for pure white, fully double, button-shaped blooms on tall, upright stems, offering a clean, bright alternative to the species' familiar blue for cutting gardens and mixed cottage borders. The white flowers pair easily with any companion color and are especially effective massed together or combined with the deep blues and maroons of other cornflower cultivars. Deadhead regularly to extend the bloom season, and expect the plants to decline with the onset of summer heat, since cornflowers are a true cool-season annual.
